entry.title: Our new research, “Disentangling the drivers of parasite occurrence in a native and a non-native small mammal across a land-use gradient”, is now available on EcoEvoRxiv!

link.title: Our new research, “Disentangling the drivers of parasite occurrence in a native and a non-native small mammal across a land-use gradient”, is now available on EcoEvoRxiv!

entry.content:
In this study, Matan and collaborators investigate the drivers of parasite occurrence in both native and non-native small mammal species across a land-use gradient in Madagascar. By comparing infection patterns between species with different evolutionary histories in the landscape, the study sheds light on how host traits, environmental context, and land-use change interact to shape parasite distributions. These findings contribute to a growing understanding of how habitat transformation affects disease dynamics at the wildlife interface.

Read the full paper here: EcoEvoRxiv

entry.title: Our new research, “Metabolite correlation networks reveal complex phenotypes of adaptation-driving mutations”, is now available on Nature Communications!

link.title: Our new research, “Metabolite correlation networks reveal complex phenotypes of adaptation-driving mutations”, is now available on Nature Communications!

entry.content:
The study, previously available as a preprint, is now published following peer-review in Nature Communications!

In this study, as part of a collaboration with Shimon Bershtein’s lab, we show that adaptive evolution can reshape the structure of metabolic networks, creating complex phenotypes that link mutations to fitness. Using a metabolically impaired E. coli strain, the team demonstrates that fitness gains arise from large-scale rewiring of metabolite correlation networks, producing smaller, more cohesive, and better-connected clusters. These results highlight metabolite correlation networks as a powerful framework for uncovering emergent phenotypes that drive metabolic adaptation.

Read the full paper here: Nature Communications

entry.title: Our new research, “Contextual evidence for categorising interactions and guiding their discovery”, is now available on EcoEvoRxiv!

link.title: Our new research, “Contextual evidence for categorising interactions and guiding their discovery”, is now available on EcoEvoRxiv!

entry.content:
In this study, Kesem and Shir introduce a framework for using contextual evidence to categorise ecological interactions and guide the discovery of unknown ones. By leveraging structural and contextual features of interaction networks, the approach offers a principled way to distinguish between different types of ecological relationships and to prioritise which missing interactions are most worth investigating in the field. This work advances the toolkit for ecologists working on large, incompletely sampled interaction networks.

Read the full paper here: EcoEvoRxiv

entry.title: Itamar Awarded a Scholarship from the Council for Higher Education!

link.title: Itamar Awarded a Scholarship from the Council for Higher Education!

entry.content: We are proud to share that Itamar Talpaz has been awarded a scholarship from the (israeli) Council for Higher Education! The scholarship will support his research on “Prediction of infectious disease structure in multiscale ecological systems”, a project that combines network science and machine learning to understand how disease risk is structured across biological scales, from host traits to ecological communities. Congratulations, Itamar!

entry.title: Our new research, “Predicting ecological interactions across space through pairwise integration of latent network patterns”, is now available on Methods in Ecology and Evolution!

link.title: Our new research, “Predicting ecological interactions across space through pairwise integration of latent network patterns”, is now available on Methods in Ecology and Evolution!

entry.content:
The study, previously available as a preprint, is now published following peer-review in Methods in Ecology and Evolution!

In this study, Kesem and the team introduce a spatially explicit network-based framework to predict missing species interactions while accounting for spatial variability in ecological communities. Applying the method to plant–pollinator networks across the Canary Islands, they show that latent network structure contains strong predictive power for identifying unobserved links. Performance was highest when drawing information from nearby, ecologically similar sites — underscoring that incorporating spatial structure is essential for reliable link prediction.

Read the full paper here: Methods in Ecology and Evolution

entry.title: Matan’s Concluding Seminar
entry.content: On June 30th, our first PhD student, Matan Markfeld gave his concluding seminar, a major milestone marking the end of his PhD journey in the lab. Matan’s research has focused on how environmental gradients and land-use changes shape the structure of ecological networks, from the microbiome to host-parasite interactions and disease transmission. His work, combining network analysis and field ecology, has been a wonderful contribution to the lab. We are proud of everything you’ve accomplished, Matan, and excited for you! Congratulations, and best of luck for what comes next!
